                How Trump's newest tariffs could impact Americans and the economy
                Nov 25, 2026 6:50 PM EST
            

        

        

    

    


            
                
    

    

                    



        
    

                
            
        
        
        

            By —

            
                
                    Lisa Desjardins
                
                
                    Lisa Desjardins

Karina Cuevas
                
                
                    Karina Cuevas

The Trump administration announced plans for a new round of tariffs on China, the European Union and 12 other major trading partners. China would face the highest rate with a new 20% tariff on most products. To discuss how this will impact Americans and the economy, Lisa Desjardins spoke with Gavin Bade of The Wall Street Journal.

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Now our other major story tonight.

The Trump administration announced plans for a new round of tariffs on China, the European Union, and 12 other major trading partners. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argues, this is to protect manufacturing in the U.S.

Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative:

We have a very consumption-driven economy, and we should be producing more of that here in the United States, but it makes it really hard when these other countries are producing or creating capacity that are not really justified by the economics of the situation.

And so we're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it.

China would face the highest rate with a new 20 percent tariff on most products. That would top existing levels, setting up a potential 40 percent tariff if negotiations fall apart. Other countries would face 10 to 20 percent in additional tariffs. Those could go into effect as soon as January.

For more on how this will impact Americans and the American economy, I'm joined by Gavin Bade of The Wall Street Journal, who first reported this plan.

Gavin, let's start with the big picture here. If these tariffs went into force in full, how significant would they be?

Gavin Bade, Trade and Economic Policy Reporter, The Wall Street Journal: I think they will be significant for consumers' pocketbooks.

This is really the Trump administration trying to rebuild its tariff wall after the Supreme Court back in February ruled many of its levies illegal. So the administration has reached for a different legal authority this time, one that is more tried and tested, and has put in place basically the level of tariffs that we saw at the beginning of this year before the Supreme Court decision.

You mentioned that Supreme Court decision. We heard from the Yale Economic Lab today, and they did say essentially, in their review, this will get us back to that level, as you put, and they think these tariffs would add another $400 for each American in general.

But my question to you is about that legal underlying rationale. How certain are we that these really have legal standing?

Well, they have certainly got a much better chance than the ones that went down at the Supreme Court.

That first round of tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, that was the first time that law had ever been used for tariffs, and the Supreme Court really looked askance at the administration trying to rewrite the entire global trading system using this emergency law.

So they have turned to this section of the Trade Act of 1974. It's called Section 301, and it's to deal with unfair trading practices from other nations. So what they're saying here, and what you heard Jamieson Greer, the trade representative, say, is that they think that other countries are unnecessarily subsidizing their industries.

That's allowing company countries like China to flood the world market with products at a very low price. That's disadvantaging U.S. producers. And so they say that tariffs in this case are justified.

I know, when you mentioned Section 301, that sounds like we're getting into sort of minutiae, but actually that's something I think our viewers are going to hear more about as we head into January.

Something else about the timing, of course, is that the so-called tariff truce with China is supposed to end in January. It's hard to overlook that timing. When you look at the announcement today, do you think this is mostly a negotiating tactic about that deadline in January?

This falls right in line with what the Trump administration has been trying to do with China. So I don't think this will blow up the trade truce in itself. This level of 20 percent tariffs, a little bit higher, on some Chinese products, that's what the Chinese have expected for a long time.

The U.S. has telegraphed this action. This investigation was monthslong, and it's really just going to get us back to the level that we were at when the truce was signed back in October 2025. So this alone won't blow up U.S.-China trade relations.

But if talks don't continue apace, and if the Chinese start to do things that the Trump administration doesn't like, then, as you noted, they can Jack this tariff up to 40 percent, and then that starts to get really, really disruptive.

China plays the long game. Is there any evidence that any of these tariff actions have influenced how China does business?

Well, I think what we have seen is, the U.S. trade deficit with regard to China has gone down. We have seen companies try to move production out of China, maybe to other Southeast Asian nations. We have seen a lot of technology manufacturing go to India, for instance.

And then there's also a problem of transshipment, or Chinese goods that are shipped through other countries, and maybe they do a small amount of work on a product in a country like Vietnam or Thailand or something, they label it as made in Vietnam, and send it to the U.S.

This is something that the Trump administration is trying to get ahold of, trying to get ahold on. There are laws on the books against transshipment, but it's a very difficult thing to track. So I think you're seeing companies responding in a number of ways, both legal and illegal, to these tariffs.

You mentioned consumers. If these tariffs were to go into effect in January, which is the earliest that that could happen, when would we feel it here as American consumers?

You know, I think there won't be a big price shock initially, right? Because we had a certain level of tariffs coming into this year. Then the Supreme Court knocked down a lot of the tariffs, so the tariff rate went lower.

But companies, from what I have been seeing, haven't been changing their pricing that much because they always knew that the Trump administration would try to jack these tariffs back up again. So I think what we have seen over the past year, year-and-a-half is, these tariffs have filtered through the U.S. economy gradually.

As companies have depleted their stockpiles of goods, they have raised prices according to the tariffs, and the U.S. consumer is paying most or almost all of the tariff price here, despite what the Trump administration says.

A last question in our final 30 seconds here. This was one of the factors, along with inflation fears, to added turbulence we saw on the stock market today. How do you see the next coming weeks for the stock market?

Yes, I think there's going to be a lot of anxiety on the stock market, not just about these tariffs, which they have probably baked into their cake, so to speak. But I think the AI trade is really under threat here, all of this controversy over Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary.

You're going to start to see congressional hearings next week. I think we could see more news about investigations into other companies that maybe have been smuggling chips into China. So, there's a lot of anxiety surrounding that trade. And so much of the market is concentrated around those AI and tech firms that, if they get a cold, everyone else is going to get sick as well.

Gavin Bade of The Wall Street Journal, thank you.

By Christopher Rugaber, Aamer Madhani, Josh Boak, Associated Press

By E. Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press

By Paul Wiseman, Associated Press

Lisa Desjardins
                
                
                    Lisa Desjardins

Lisa Desjardins is a correspondent for PBS News Hour, where she covers news from the U.S. Capitol while also traveling across the country to report on how decisions in Washington affect people where they live and work.
